newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zulu leader urges more rights for S.Africa chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Zulu leader urges more rights for S.Africa chiefs.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela's main black opposition leader urged traditional leaders on Friday to oppose South Africa's new constitutional blueprint, saying it was bent on destroying their "God-given" authority.
Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, speaking at a meeting of tribal leaders in the Indian Ocean city of Durban, also told Mandela's government to stop "meddling" with traditional rule.
He said this was capable of wrecking the 2-1/2-year-old democracy and creating conflicts which could "bring the country to its knees".

"We must together find the strength to reject a constitution which does not protect traditional leaders and local government, and requires no recognition for our indigenous law," Buthelezi told about 500 chiefs and headmen from across the country.
"We can rise to the challenge ahead, and resist those who are bent on destroying us...We are not at liberty to relinquish the duties for which we were born."

He said the blueprint of the final constitution took away the right embodied in the interim constitution of automatic office status for chiefs in local governments and the right to be trustees and administators of communal land.

"South Africa cannot be built on the triumph of westernised realites...which regard African realities as an inferior form of societal organisation...," the IFP leader said to applause from the predominantly male audience.

The IFP walked out of the Constitutional Assembly (CA) early last year in a row over the powers of provincial governments and was the only one of seven parties in parliament not there when the draft final constitution was adopted in May.

The 11-judge Constitutional Court recently returned the final draft to the CA, saying inadequate powers had been allocated to provinces and that measures to protect a proposed Bill of Rights against arbitrary amendment were too weak.
The CA has until October 7 to finalise amendments to the constitution, in line with the court's 160-page judgment. The IFP is currently reviewing its boycott of the assembly.
South Africa's final post-apartheid constitution is expected to come into effect early in 1997.
